body: Take a few minutes after you read a selection to write a brief summary and then add two facts and examples.
Create short quizzes to test your understanding of the material you have read for each assignment.
Learn the elements of a diagram and then recreate it from memory on a blank page. Check accuracy and edit, if necessary.
Turn the bold titles of the chapter into questions. Answer by writing notes in the margin. Focus on main ideas, then on facts.
Use standard abbreviations or create your own when writing notes based on textbooks or articles.
Highlight text only after you say or rephrase and then write it in your own words in the margins, endnotes, or note cards.
Read when you are most rested and alert—and least distracted. You’ll learn faster, greater, and enjoy better retention.
View vocabulary as a basic building block of comprehension and use illustrations to help understand and memorize meaning.
Focus attention by reading to answer questions or searching for key words and phrases. Repeat information in your own words.
Define a purpose for reading and then select a strategy for that purpose. Ask, “Should I survey, skim, or read closely?”
Create diagrams and charts after you read a selection. This enhances your comprehension and retention.
Read an assignment or article and discuss with a study partner the main ideas, facts, and implications.
Distinguish between reading to understand a concept and memorizing the information for use later.
Generate questions from the lecture titles. This provides a purpose for reading and an overview of the material.
Read the introduction, illustrations and summary as a preview of the assignment and recite the main ideas in your own words.
Increase reading rate by reading newspaper articles rapidly to answer  the questions “who, what, where, when, why?”
Increase reading rate by reading an interesting and easy novel for 15 minutes each day. Focus on plot and character.
Do word and crossword puzzles to improve vocabulary and word usage. Use the dictionary to learn unfamiliar words.
Read the front page of a newspaper each day and discuss with a friend the main ideas and a few facts about one article.
Read a newspaper article and then listen to the radio and television versions. Compare the amount of background and detail.
Read the assignment, relate it to the syllabus, then, list ways it reflects the objectives of the course.
Review your lecture notes to identify main ideas that involve the writing assignment. Generate a few questions.
Generate questions to answer in a paper and write key words or ideas to  answer each question.
Answer each question to address in your paper by writing the main idea, a further explanation, two facts, and an example.
Get ready to write by allowing time to brainstorm. Use images or just begin writing notes about a word or idea.
Trigger creativity by finding quotes related to important vocabulary words in your course or assignment.
Work with a partner or small group to consider and flesh out ideas for papers and projects.
Before setting pen to page, allow 5 to 10 minutes to review your ideas, perhaps creating a diagram or chart.
Only engage in brainstorming activities when you are rested and alert. Fatigue reduces rather than enhances creativity.
Separate your brainstorming activities from times during which you analyze, outline, or write your ideas.
Write for brief periods, perhaps 20 to 40 minutes; take a short 5– to 10– minute break, then resume writing.
Plan to complete a paper or presentation at least one day prior to the due date to allow for final editing.
Use a template or software program to write your bibliography so that all the information is formatted accurately.
Know what you want to say before you write. Ask a question and answer it aloud before you write.
Read each sentence aloud to spot spelling and grammar mistakes as well as excess wording.
Check that you have sufficient facts, citations, and examples to support each major point of your paper.
Always give proper credit for another’s work by using direct quotes and citing author, date, publisher and page numbers.
Date and back up every revision of your paper on a thumb or external drive or email it to yourself.
Pose questions and discuss the answers using a voice recorder. Write after you listen to the recording.
Make a timeline and check off writing activities such as time to think, brainstorm, write, revise and edit.
Get feedback from your instructor about a proposed paper. Discuss your proposed topic, questions to address and references.
Begin by answering one question, even if it is in the middle of the paper. This spurs action and avoids writer’s block.
Cool down before you begin to begin to write. Visualize a successful experience; take 2 to 4 deep breaths and stretch.
After breaks, gear up before restarting. Review notes, visualize the completed paper, and identify a small goal.
Check your organization by marking the main idea sentence of each paragraph with a colored pencil.
Prevent panic and remain calm during tests by taking four deep breaths and a few stretches every 15 minutes.
Don’t spend too much time on any one question. This ensures that you finish the test and get the most points possible.
Review the test to find the easiest questions. This reduces stress and allows time to avoid silly mistakes.
Awake early before a test to make sure you eat a healthy breakfast and feel refreshed.
Review the results of tests so you can practice the subjects or types of questions on which you did least well.
